title: The Two Abjurations: from Taurisano to the Place du Salin
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Terra d'Otranto and the Studium of Naples

stops.name: Taurisano, the birth in Terra d'Otranto
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by EN and IT; it.wikipedia gives 19 or 20 January and hedges between the two days
stops.campa: In the heel of the Kingdom of Naples, in a town of olive groves and salt light between two seas, a son is born to Giovan Battista Vanini, a businessman out of Tuscan Tresana, and to a mother of the Spanish house of Lopez de Noguera. They christen him Lucilio. The Terra d'Otranto he is born into is Spanish-governed, Greek-haunted, thick with parish clergy, and he will spend his first fourteen years inside it. The Italian record gives the birth as the nineteenth of January, or else the twentieth, and has never settled which.
suggested_refs: The Vanini birth-house at Taurisano, still standing and marked in the town

stops.name: Naples, enrollment at the Studium
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At fourteen he comes up to Naples and enters the Studium, the oldest state university in Europe, in the quarter of narrow streets behind San Domenico Maggiore where law, medicine and theology are argued half in the open. The city is the largest in Spanish Italy and among the most crowded in Christendom, and its lecture halls carry an Aristotelianism that reads Averroes and Pomponazzi with more attention than Rome likes. He is put to civil and canon law. No reachable source names the hall he sat in, only the quarter it stood in.
suggested_refs: The university quarter behind San Domenico Maggiore, Naples, seat of the Studium in 1599

stops.name: Naples, the Carmelite habit and the name Fra Gabriele
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the religious name by EN and IT; the convent is a traditional identification only and is therefore a reconstruction
stops.campa: Four years into his studies he takes the habit of the Carmelites and with it a new name, Fra Gabriele. Which house of the order received him is recorded nowhere reachable; tradition points to Santa Maria del Carmine Maggiore, the great Carmelite church by the market where the order has stood since the thirteenth century, and tradition is all there is. What the vows change is his standing, not his reading. He remains a law student, now under obedience to a prior, and Fra Gabriele is the name he answers to until 1612.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria del Carmine Maggiore, Naples, the traditional but unverified house of his profession

stops.name: Naples, the doctorate in utroque iure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by EN and IT; the day is not given and is defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In June he takes the doctorate in utroque iure, in both laws, canon and civil, the double qualification that opens the ecclesiastical courts and any tribunal in Catholic Europe. He is twenty-one. Nothing in the degree suggests natural philosophy and nothing in it forbids one; what it supplies is a training in arguing both sides of a case in two jurisdictions, and that habit will be read against him at the end as duplicity. The month is attested and the day is not, so the record has him a doctor of both laws sometime in June 1606.
suggested_refs: The doctoral formula in utroque iure, canon and civil law together, as conferred at Naples

stops.name: Naples, the death of the father
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sources give an approximate year only, with no month and no place beyond the general one
stops.campa: Around the same year Giovan Battista Vanini dies. The record gives a year and little else: no month, no deathbed, no account of what passed to the son who had left Taurisano at fourteen and taken vows at eighteen. Whatever inheritance or obligation the death carried does not appear again in anything written about him. The Tuscan merchant who came south into the Terra d'Otranto leaves behind a Carmelite friar with a law degree, a religious name, and no visible property.
suggested_refs: The Tresana origin of the Vanini family, given by it.wikipedia and otherwise undocumented

segments.name: Padua: the Carmine, Sarpi's City, and the Lenten Sermons

stops.name: Padua, the Carmine and the theology course
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by en.wikipedia; it.wikipedia gives no year at all for the transfer, so the 1603 date sometimes quoted is an inference and is not carried here
stops.campa: The order sends him north to Padua for theology, to the convent attached to Santa Maria del Carmine, which the Carmelites have held since 1300 and will hold until 1806. Padua is Venetian ground, and Venetian ground in these years means something particular: the Republic has just come out of an interdict war with Paul V, and its clergy have learned to argue in public that a pope's authority stops at the edge of temporal things. Vanini arrives into the middle of that argument at twenty-three.
suggested_refs: The Carmelite complex at Padua, held by the order 1300-1806, at 45.4132, 11.8741

stops.name: Padua, the university and the Lenten sermons
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sermons and the year by EN and IT; no church is named and the day within Lent is unrecorded
stops.campa: He studies theology in the university that had taught Pomponazzi's Aristotle, and he is drawn toward the circle around Paolo Sarpi, the Servite who wrote Venice's case against the pope. In Lent he preaches, and what he says from the pulpit reaches authorities who begin keeping a file on him. No sermon of his survives, only the judgment of the men who heard it. Of Pomponazzi, whose doctrine of the mortal soul a Lateran Council had condemned in the century before his birth, he will write in print: my master, my divine teacher, prince of the philosophers of our age.
stops.quote: magister meus, divinus praeceptor meus, nostri seculi Philosophorum princeps
stops.quote_source: Vanini on Pietro Pomponazzi, De Admirandis Naturae Reginae Deaeque Mortalium Arcanis (Paris, 1616), as quoted on en.wikipedia
suggested_refs: Paolo Sarpi's Venetian circle, 1606-1612, and the interdict controversy Vanini walked into

stops.name: Padua, expelled from the convent
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by it.wikipedia, 'nel gennaio 1612 allontanato da Padova'; the day is not given
stops.campa: In January he is put out of the Padua convent for anti-papal attitudes, and his superior orders him back to Naples. He does not go. Nine years of the habit end in one administrative sentence, and the man who walks out of the cloister is a doctor of both laws with no benefice and no protector. The article that records the expulsion, "nel gennaio 1612 allontanato da Padova", then has him fleeing to England the year after, which its own July date makes impossible.
sources: Wikipedia (IT), 'Giulio Cesare Vanini' (internal inconsistency flagged in the report)
suggested_refs: The Carmelite obedience recalling him to Naples, January 1612, refused

segments.name: The Road North: Flight to England

stops.name: Venice, the English embassy
stops.date_confidence: attested that he took refuge with the English ambassador; no month is given, and the embassy residence is unidentified so the pin is a general city coordinate
stops.campa: He goes down to Venice and puts himself under the protection of the English ambassador. Unhappy friars have been using that door out of Catholic Italy for a decade, and everyone on the Rialto knows what walking through it means. Which house on which canal, nobody wrote down. He leaves it with a companion, Bonaventura Genocchi, a fellow Carmelite, and with a plan to reach a country where the pope has no jurisdiction. The month of the departure is nowhere given.
suggested_refs: The English embassy at Venice under Dudley Carleton, refuge of Italian religious in flight

stops.name: Bologna, the first stage of the flight
stops.date_confidence: attested as a named stage of the route by it.wikipedia; no date within the year is given, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The two friars go west through Bologna, papal territory governed by a legate, where a Carmelite absent without leave is a man with something to explain. Whether they travel in habit or out of it the sources do not say, and nobody wrote down where they slept or who paid for it. What the sources give is a bare list of places strung along a line that runs the length of Italy and then the length of the Rhine. Bologna is the first name on that list, and the second is Milan.
suggested_refs: The route Padua-Bologna-Milan-Grisons-Rhine-Netherlands-England, given as a list and nothing more

stops.name: Milan, the road west and north
stops.date_confidence: attested as a named stage of the route by it.wikipedia; no date within the year, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: From Bologna the road bends north-west into Spanish Lombardy, into the city of Carlo Borromeo's successors, where the Inquisition is efficient and the archbishop's police are better organized than most. Milan is the last great Catholic capital before the passes. Beyond it the ground changes: the Alps, then Protestant valleys where a runaway friar is a curiosity rather than a crime. Genocchi is still with him, and nothing is written of what either man carried out of Italy.
suggested_refs: Spanish Milan in 1612, last Catholic administration on the road to the Alpine passes

stops.name: Chur, crossing the Grisons
stops.date_confidence: attested that the route crossed the Swiss Grisons; no town is named in the sources, and Chur stands for the crossing
stops.campa: They cross into the Grisons, the league of Protestant valleys that controls the passes between Lombardy and the Rhine and that Rome has been trying to recover for a generation. Here the confessional ground turns over under their feet. A Carmelite in flight becomes, in a single day's walking, a man among people who consider his order an abuse and his vows void, and who have no machinery for sending him back to it. The road out of the mountains follows the young Rhine, and the two of them follow the road.
suggested_refs: The Grisons passes in 1612, contested ground between Venice, Spain and the Protestant leagues

stops.name: Cologne, the Rhine road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sources name only the Rhine, Germany and the Netherlands, so Cologne is a representative waypoint on that route and not a confirmed stop
stops.campa: The route runs down the Rhine through German and then Dutch territory toward the sea. No town on that river is named in anything reachable, and Cologne stands here for a passage the sources describe only as a direction. The river carries wine barges, soldiers and confessional refugees in both directions, in the last quiet years before the Empire goes to war for thirty of them. Somewhere on it two Italian friars, one a doctor of canon law, are working their way toward a boat for England.
sources: Wikipedia (IT), 'Giulio Cesare Vanini' (route given only as the Rhine, Germany, the Netherlands)
suggested_refs: The Rhine corridor as an escape route for Italian religious exiles, c. 1600-1620

stops.name: London, lodged at Lambeth Palace
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia; no month is given for the arrival, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He arrives in London and is lodged at Lambeth Palace, the archbishop's house across the river from Westminster, under the protection of George Abbot. The English church has a use for Italian converts, who are living proof that Rome loses the men who think, and Abbot houses him, feeds him, and expects a public act in return. The Thames runs past the garden wall. Which month he came ashore no source gives; the abjuration in July is the first dated thing that happens to him in England.
suggested_refs: Lambeth Palace under Archbishop George Abbot, host to continental converts

stops.name: London, the abjuration at the Italian Church
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by EN and IT; the congregation's meeting-place in the City at that date is unconfirmed and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: In July, before the Italian Protestant congregation in the City, he renounces the Church of Rome and takes the Church of England. The Italian article puts Francis Bacon in the room as a witness, which would set the Solicitor General of England watching a Neapolitan friar unmake his vows in a hall among London's exiled Lucchese silk-weavers. Vanini is twenty-seven, and it is the first of two public changes of religion. Whether Bacon stood in that hall at all rests on the Italian article and on nothing else.
sources: Wikipedia (IT), 'Giulio Cesare Vanini' (Bacon as witness, single-source)
suggested_refs: The Italian Protestant congregation of London, refuge of Lucchese and Venetian exiles
francis_bacon.journey.json, for Bacon's London years

segments.name: England: the Second Turn and the Gatehouse

stops.name: Cambridge, the visit to the university
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: EN and IT record the visit with no date, purpose or circumstance; the year is the one they imply
stops.campa: He goes to Cambridge. That is very nearly the whole of it: the sources say he visited the university and stop there. What he did, whom he saw, whether he lectured or listened or was shown about as a trophy convert, no reachable source records. It is one of two English gaps in a life otherwise documented by the men who arrested him. Did anyone in the colleges know they were being shown a friar who had abjured Rome in July, or was he simply a foreign scholar passing through in term time?
suggested_refs: The unexplained English university visits of 1613, recorded without detail in every source

stops.name: Oxford, the second university
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the visit is recorded without date or circumstance, exactly as at Cambridge
stops.campa: Oxford is the second name on the same bare line. Both universities are noted, neither described. In this same year he is writing secretly to Rome, asking to be taken back into the Catholic Church as a secular priest, so the man walking these quadrangles has already decided that his English career is finished. Rome grants the request. He goes on for a while longer on Anglican hospitality, with a papal permission in his pocket and no benefice on either side of the Channel.
suggested_refs: The 1613 petition to Rome, running concurrently with his English hospitality

stops.name: London, the secret appeal to Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by en.wikipedia; no month is given, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The quarrel with his hosts comes, and he answers it by writing to the pope. He asks to be readmitted to the Catholic Church, not as a Carmelite under a rule that had expelled him, but as a secular priest answerable to a bishop and to no prior. In the space of a year he has abjured Catholicism in public and petitioned to return to it in private. Rome grants the petition, and it is the private half that his English protectors find out about. Nothing in the record says which of the two he meant.
suggested_refs: The status of secular priest, sought as an exit from Carmelite obedience

stops.name: Westminster, arrest and the Gatehouse prison
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by en.wikipedia; the detail that the arrest followed a service and that he was held at the Gatehouse is single-source and is a reconstruction
stops.campa: In January Archbishop Abbot has him arrested, by the Italian account after a religious service, and he is put in the Gatehouse, the prison built into the precinct wall at Westminster Abbey. The French article says forty-nine days, for attacks on the Anglican church, a figure no other source gives and one that does not fit the January-to-March interval it is fastened to. Lambeth Palace, where the archbishop had housed and fed him eighteen months before, stands a few hundred yards upriver from the cell.
suggested_refs: The Gatehouse prison at Westminster Abbey, demolished 1776

stops.name: Westminster, the escape from the Gatehouse
stops.date_confidence: attested to a window: it.wikipedia gives between 10 and 16 March 1614, en.wikipedia gives March without a range; the Spanish ambassador's help is single-source
stops.campa: Between the tenth and the sixteenth of March he gets out. The Italian account credits the Spanish ambassador, whose embassy in London ran a standing traffic in Catholics lifted out of English prisons and whose interest in a repentant Italian friar needs no explaining. How he left the Gatehouse, through which gate, on whose money, the record does not say; the English article gives only the month. He is next heard of on the far side of the Channel, standing in front of a papal nuncio.
suggested_refs: The Spanish embassy in London as an extraction channel for imprisoned Catholics

segments.name: Back Inside the Church: Brussels, Paris, Genoa

stops.name: Brussels, before the nuncio Bentivoglio
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by it.wikipedia; the day is not given
stops.campa: In April he presents himself at Brussels to Guido Bentivoglio, papal nuncio to the Spanish Netherlands, a Ferrarese who will one day be a cardinal and write the standard history of the Flemish wars. The interview is the first stage of a negotiated return. Vanini has a papal permission from the year before and an English prison behind him, and both are usable: the escape makes him a confessor of a kind, the permission makes him regularizable. Bentivoglio passes him on toward Paris.
suggested_refs: Guido Bentivoglio's nunciature to Flanders, 1607-1615, and his Della guerra di Fiandra

stops.name: Paris, the nuncio Ubaldini and the defense of Trent
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by it.wikipedia; en.wikipedia dates the Tridentine writing loosely to the summer
stops.campa: In May he is in Paris, presented to Roberto Ubaldini, nuncio to France, and he writes what the moment requires: a commentary in defense of the Council of Trent, subscribing to its principles. The Italian article dates this to May and the English only to that summer. It is the exact opposite of everything the Padua sermons had been suspected of. The text survives in no reachable form, so it cannot be set beside the two books he prints next, and whether he meant a word of it is a question the record does not answer.
suggested_refs: The lost Commentari in difesa del Concilio di Trento, known only by its title

stops.name: Rome, the disputed summons
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, contradiction unresolved: en.wikipedia has him travel to Rome to answer before the Inquisition; neither the Italian nor the French account contains the journey. No date within the year is given
stops.campa: The English account sends him to Rome in this year to answer for the London apostasy before the Inquisition. The Italian and French accounts do not. They take him from Brussels and Paris straight toward the Genoese coast without a word about the Holy Office, and nothing reconciles the two versions. The pin stands here because one encyclopedia puts him here and because a man in his position would ordinarily have been summoned. Whether he ever stood in that building is genuinely unknown.
sources: Wikipedia (EN), 'Lucilio Vanini' (against the silence of IT and FR)
suggested_refs: The Palazzo del Sant'Uffizio, Rome, where the summons would have been answered if it happened

stops.name: Lecce, the disputed return
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, contradiction unresolved: fr.wikipedia alone has him return to Lecce and reconcile with the Church, adding a stay at Geneva; EN and IT place him in Genoa across the same months
stops.campa: One account, and only one, brings him home. The French article has him return to the Terra d'Otranto, to Lecce a few hours from the town where he was born, formally reconcile with the Catholic Church, and turn to the natural sciences of the age. The English and Italian articles have him in Genoa across exactly those months, teaching philosophy for his bread. Both cannot be true. The Lecce homecoming rests on the French article alone, which adds to it a stay at Geneva that no other source mentions.
sources: Wikipedia (FR), 'Lucilio Vanini' (single source, contradicted by EN and IT)
suggested_refs: Lecce and Taurisano, the Terra d'Otranto he may or may not have seen again

stops.name: Genoa, teaching the sons of Scipione Doria
stops.date_confidence: attested by EN and IT for a stay of some months; the month within 1614 is inferred from the summer dating
stops.campa: He lives some months in Genoa, finds Genocchi again, and earns his bread teaching philosophy to the sons of Scipione Doria, in the city the Doria have run for a century out of the palaces of the Strada Nuova, built on Spanish silver. A tutor in a great house is invisible in a way a preacher is not, and for a season nobody writes anything down about him. It is the last settled work of his life that anyone pays him for openly and under his own name. The stay runs from the summer into the following January.
suggested_refs: The Doria palaces of the Strada Nuova, Genoa, where he tutored in 1614

stops.name: Genoa, the arrest of Genocchi
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by en.wikipedia; the day is not given
stops.campa: In January the Inquisition takes Genocchi in Genoa. The two had left Padua together, crossed the Alps together, gone down the Rhine together and come back into Italy by different roads, and now one of them is in a cell. Vanini does not wait to hear what is said under questioning. He leaves the city and crosses into France. Bonaventura Genocchi drops out of the record at the moment the Inquisition takes him, and nothing reachable says what became of him afterward.
suggested_refs: The Inquisition sweep of 1615 against friars returned from England

segments.name: Lyon and Paris: the Two Books

stops.name: Lyon, the Amphitheatrum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication by EN and IT; the day is not given
stops.campa: In June the Lyon presses print the Amphitheatrum Aeternae Providentiae Divino-Magicum, a defense of eternal providence against atheists, epicureans, peripatetics and stoics. It is built as a set of exercitationes in which the objections are stated at their full strength and the refutations are not always the longer half. Readers have argued ever since over whether the book smuggles in what it pretends to demolish. Copies of the manuscript will end up in Stuttgart and in Hamburg.
stops.quote: Se Dio vuole i peccati, allora è lui che li commette; se non li vuole, essi vengono tuttavia commessi. Quindi o egli è imprevidente o impotente, oppure è crudele, perché o non sa o trascura di compiere quello che vuole.
stops.quote_source: Amphitheatrum Aeternae Providentiae, exercitatio 16, p. 103, in the Italian rendering given on it.wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Amphitheatrum manuscripts preserved at Stuttgart and Hamburg

stops.name: Paris, the protection of Bassompierre
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: it.wikipedia names Bassompierre only as a power at Marie de' Medici's court and as the dedicatee of De Admirandis. The often-repeated chaplaincy is unsourced, and he was not yet a Marshal of France
stops.campa: In Paris he attaches himself to Francois de Bassompierre, colonel-general of the Swiss and Grisons, a man powerful at the court of Marie de' Medici and not yet the marshal that later accounts make him. What the connection was in practice is nowhere documented. The claim that Vanini served as his chaplain appears in no source that can be checked. What can be checked is a dedication. The book he is finishing will carry Bassompierre's name on its first page, and a colonel-general's name on a first page is a form of armor.
suggested_refs: The dedication of De Admirandis to Bassompierre, the only documented tie between the two men

stops.name: Paris, De Admirandis printed by Adrien Perier
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by EN and IT; the day is not given
stops.campa: In September the Protestant printer Adrien Perier brings out De Admirandis Naturae Reginae Deaeque Mortalium Arcanis, dialogues on the secrets of nature, queen and goddess of mortals. Two theologians of the Sorbonne have read it and approved it. It discusses the generation of living things, oracles, the origin of religions and the physical causes of prophecy, and it does all of this in the mouths of two speakers, so that nothing in the book is said in the author's own voice.
stops.quote_source: De Admirandis Naturae Reginae Deaeque Mortalium Arcanis (Paris, 1616), quoted in the biographical dictionary article 'Vanini' on fr.wikisource
suggested_refs: Adrien Perier's Paris imprint of 1616, a Protestant press printing a Catholic priest's dialogues

stops.name: Paris, the Sorbonne withdraws its approval
stops.date_confidence: inferred: it.wikipedia says only that the approval was withdrawn shortly after publication and gives no month, so October is an editorial placement
stops.campa: Shortly after publication the two theologians withdraw their approval, saying the printed text is not the text they read. Inside the dialogues a speaker has already admitted, of the orthodox defense Vanini published at Lyon the year before, that he had put no faith in a line of it. That admission is the retraction his second book makes of his first, and it is in print under an approval the Sorbonne can no longer stand behind. The book is condemned to be burned.
stops.quote: J'ai écrit beaucoup de choses dans l'Amphithéâtre auxquelles je n'ajoute pas la moindre foi
stops.quote_source: Attributed self-admission within De Admirandis Naturae, quoted in the biographical dictionary article 'Vanini' on fr.wikisource
suggested_refs: Francois Garasse's 1623 judgment on the writings, reported at second hand on it.wikipedia

stops.name: Paris, the murder of Concini and the flight
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by EN and IT, which tie the flight to the Concini assassination of 24 April 1617
stops.campa: On the drawbridge of the Louvre the king's guards shoot Concino Concini, the Florentine favorite who has governed France through the queen mother, and the court turns over in a morning. Marie de' Medici is sent to Blois. Every client of her household becomes a suspect, and Vanini's patron belongs to that household. A condemned book and an Italian name are bad enough in such a week; a protector on the losing side of a palace killing is worse. He leaves the capital and goes west.
suggested_refs: The assassination of Concino Concini, 24 April 1617, and the fall of the Medici household

segments.name: Brittany, the South, and the Assumed Name

stops.name: Redon, the abbey of Saint-Sauveur
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by en.wikipedia, which names Redon among the Breton abbeys; no month is given
stops.campa: He goes to ground in Brittany, in the abbey of Saint-Sauveur at Redon on the Vilaine, a house nine centuries old where the river meets the marsh country. An abbey is the one place in France where a man holding a papal permission to serve as a secular priest can sit still and be fed without explaining himself twice. It is the quietest year of his adult life and almost nothing is recorded of it. English Wikipedia names Redon; the other accounts say only Brittany. Then he starts moving south.
suggested_refs: The abbey of Saint-Sauveur at Redon, Breton refuge of 1617

stops.name: Guyenne and Languedoc, the Berthier household
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the pin: no town is named for the Berthier household, and a regional coordinate stands in for an unidentified site
stops.campa: He crosses Guyenne and Languedoc, tutoring in the house of a Monsieur de Berthier, in which town no source will say. Surveillance thickens around him as he goes. In these provinces the Catholic reconquest is being pressed hard against a Protestant countryside, and the men doing the pressing are exactly the magistrates and clergy who notice a foreign tutor with opinions. Rumors get around the house, and what they said was never written down, only that they were enough. He is dismissed.
suggested_refs: The unidentified Berthier household of Guyenne, last employment before Toulouse

stops.name: Toulouse, the protection of Adrien de Monluc
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the protection is attested by fr.wikipedia, which in the same sentence records that Monluc's role in the arrest is disputed; no source places Vanini at the town of Caraman
stops.campa: In Toulouse he finds a protector: Adrien de Monluc-Montesquiou, comte de Carmain, a great lord of Languedoc with a taste for wit, libertine company and printed satire, who held the county through his wife's Foix-Caraman inheritance. The article that records the protection records in the same breath that Monluc's part in the arrest raises questions. Was the last shelter of Vanini's life also the trap laid for him? The papers that could settle it were not kept, and nobody since has established it either way.
suggested_refs: Adrien de Monluc's Toulouse circle, patron of libertine wit and, possibly, of the informer

stops.name: Toulouse, teaching under the name Pomponio Uciglio
stops.date_confidence: attested that he taught in Toulouse under an assumed name; the forename is rendered variously as Pomponio, Pompeo and Lucilio across the sources
stops.campa: He teaches in Toulouse as Pomponio Uciglio, and students come to him. Toulouse is a parlement city, a university city, and the most fiercely Catholic capital in the south, where the Inquisition's memory is long and the magistrates are sons of the men who fought the Wars of Religion to a standstill in these streets. A foreign philosopher under an invented surname draws the two things that cannot safely be had together here, a following and attention. He is thirty-three years old.
suggested_refs: The alias Pomponio Uciglio, under which he taught and under which he was first sought

stops.name: Toulouse, the arrest after a month's search
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left open: it.wikipedia gives 2 August 1618 after a month-long search, en.wikipedia gives August without the day, fr.wikipedia gives November 1618
stops.campa: They hunt him a month and take him on the second of August, if the Italian date is the right one; the English article gives only the month, and the French gives November. He is questioned on his identity, his religion and his morals, three headings under which a man who has changed churches twice, taught under a false name and printed a book the Sorbonne condemned has very little room to move. It was written to prove providence and it is read to prove atheism. The Amphitheatrum lies open on the table in front of him.
stops.quote: Se Dio non volesse che nel mondo avessero luogo le peggiori e le più indegne azioni, senza alcun dubbio egli, con un solo cenno, caccerebbe e bandirebbe dai confini del mondo tutte le azioni ignominiose: chi di noi può opporre resistenza alla volontà divina?
stops.quote_source: Amphitheatrum Aeternae Providentiae, exercitatio 16, p. 104, in the Italian rendering given on it.wikiquote
suggested_refs: The three-way disagreement on the arrest date, printed side by side in the report

stops.name: Toulouse, the Palais du Parlement and the sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pin is the Palais du Parlement, not the Chateau Narbonnais, which had been demolished by 1556 and is sometimes given in error
stops.campa: The Parlement of Toulouse condemns him in February. The English summary of the charges is atheism and blasphemy; the French adds impiety, sorcery and the corruption of morals. Among the men who bring it about is Guillaume de Catel, conseiller in this same parlement and, in his other life, the antiquary who will write the history of Languedoc. The sentence is read in the palace the court built on the ground of the old counts' castle: the tongue cut out, then strangling, then burning, all of it in one afternoon.
suggested_refs: Guillaume de Catel, Memoires de l'histoire du Languedoc, by the conseiller who helped condemn him

stops.name: Toulouse, Place du Salin: the amende honorable refused
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the words are given verbatim by it.wikipedia as his answer at the amende honorable, but the page's only footnote is a popular web article of 2021, not trial documentation
stops.campa: He is brought to the salt-market square in a shirt, with a torch, to make the amende honorable: to kneel and beg pardon of God, of the King, and of justice, in that order, before the rest of the sentence is carried out. The words attributed to his refusal have been quoted for four centuries and rest, in the end, on a single footnote to a popular article of 2021. What is certain is that no pardon was obtained, because everything after it proceeded. No trial record reachable today contains the words at all.
stops.quote: Quanto a Dio non credo affatto che esista; quanto al Re non l'ho mai offeso; e quanto alla giustizia, che i diavoli, se ce ne sono, la mandino in rovina.
stops.quote_source: Traditionally attributed to Vanini at the amende honorable, Toulouse, 9 February 1619, as given on it.wikipedia
sources: Wikipedia (IT), 'Giulio Cesare Vanini' (footnoted only to Caponetto, litis.it, 2021)
suggested_refs: The amende honorable as a legal form: pardon of God, King and justice, in that order

stops.name: Toulouse, Place du Salin: the tongue and the fire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by EN, FR and IT; the detail that he refused to put out his tongue and that pincers were needed is single-source and is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The executioner takes the tongue first. One account says he would not put it out and that it had to be drawn with pincers. Then the strangling, then the fire, and the body burned to ashes in front of the square. Gabriel de Gramond, a magistrate of this same parlement who would later write the reign's history, was there or close enough to it, and left the one sentence about the sound on which everything else ever written about Vanini's death has been built. He is thirty-four.
stops.quote: jamais on n'entendit un cri plus horrible ; on auroit cru entendre le mugissement d'un bœuf qu'on tue.
stops.quote_source: Gabriel Barthelemy de Gramond, Historiarum Galliae ab excessu Henrici IV, Book XVIII (1643), in the French rendering quoted on fr.wikipedia
suggested_refs: Ettore Ferrari's medallion portrait of Vanini on the base of the Bruno monument, Campo de' Fiori, Rome, unveiled 9 June 1889, with a portrait of Luther hidden inside it and found by Lars Berggren in 1991
Arthur Schopenhauer's citation of Vanini on determinism, 1839
Leibniz to Christian Kortholt on the apology for Vanini

stops.name: Toulouse, Place du Salin: the square swept clean
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: it.wikipedia alone reports the clearing, and the ducal wedding it names took place at the Louvre in Paris on 10 February 1619, not in Toulouse
stops.campa: The next day the square is cleared in haste for a celebration of the duke of Savoy's wedding, which was in fact being held at the Louvre in Paris, where a thirteen-year-old daughter of France was married to Victor Amadeus. One source only reports the clearing at all. What became of the ashes nobody wrote down: not scattered on the Garonne, not buried, not kept, simply unrecorded. The plaque naming him at the western corner of this square went up in 2007.
suggested_refs: The 2007 plaque at the Place du Salin to 'penseurs precurseurs des Lumieres, victimes de l'obscurantisme', naming Vanini with Etienne Dolet and Michel Servet
The Espace Giulio-Cesare-Vanini, designated at the square's western corner by municipal decision of 26 November 2010
The two anonymous publications of May and June 1619 that first named him publicly as the author of De Admirandis
